Your strawberry frosting containing FD&C Red No. 3 must stop being manufactured with that color additive by January 15, 2027. On that date, the removal of 21 CFR 74.303 (the listing authorizing FD&C Red No. 3 in food) takes effect, and all existing certificates for batches of FD&C Red No. 3 cease to be effective for use in food (90 FR 4628; 91 FR 50475). The administrative stay that was in place from February 18, 2025, was lifted on August 5, 2026, and the January 15, 2027 effective date was confirmed (91 FR 50475).

Regarding product already on shelves: The January 2025 order explicitly addresses this. Per 90 FR 4628: 'When FD&C Red No. 3 has been used in food or ingested drugs while its certificate is still effective, such food or ingested drugs will not be regarded as adulterated by reason of the use of such color additive.' This means frosting manufactured and colored with FD&C Red No. 3 before January 15, 2027 — while the certificate was still effective — is NOT rendered adulterated after that date. However, any food colored with FD&C Red No. 3 after January 15, 2027 will be considered adulterated because the color additive will be uncertified and its use unauthorized.

Note: The January 2025 order sets no separate compliance date; the operative deadline is derived from the effective date of January 15, 2027. There is no sell-through or phase-out period stated — the distinction is solely based on when the color additive was used (i.e., incorporated into the food), not when the finished product is sold.

answer_rows.trigger: Revocation of 21 CFR 74.303 (FD&C Red No. 3 listing for food use)
answer_rows.required_change: Reformulate to remove FD&C Red No. 3; all manufacturing using this color additive must cease before the effective date. Product manufactured with FD&C Red No. 3 while its certificate was still effective (before January 15, 2027) is not adulterated.

response.answer: No, the HHS request to phase out Red No. 3 sooner than 2027 is not binding on you. The binding legal instrument is the final order published on January 16, 2025 (90 FR 4628, Doc. 2025-00830), which revokes the color additive listing for FD&C Red No. 3 in food (21 CFR 74.303) with an effective date of January 15, 2027. The order was administratively stayed from February 18, 2025, through August 5, 2026, and the stay was lifted by the document published at 91 FR 50475 (Doc. 2026-15920), which confirmed the original effective dates unchanged. An HHS press statement or request asking manufacturers to voluntarily phase out use earlier than the effective date is guidance or a policy preference, not a legally binding requirement. Only the final order carries the force of law. Under the confirmed effective date of January 15, 2027, food containing FD&C Red No. 3 will be deemed adulterated after that date (90 FR 4628 at section VI). No separate compliance date is stated in the order; the operative deadline is derived from the effective date of January 15, 2027. Until that date, use of FD&C Red No. 3 in food while its certification remains effective does not render the food adulterated (2025-00830, section VI). You are not legally required to act before January 15, 2027, regardless of any non-binding HHS request.

response.answer: Under the updated 'healthy' nutrient content claim rule (89 FR 106064, Doc. 2024-29957), a food must generally meet two main criteria: (1) it must contain a specified amount of a food group equivalent (FGE) from food groups encouraged by the Dietary Guidelines, 2020–2025 (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, fat-free and low-fat dairy, lean meat, seafood, eggs, beans, peas, lentils, nuts, and seeds), and (2) it must not exceed specified nutrient-to-limit (NTL) thresholds for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium, based on a percentage of the Daily Value for those nutrients. As stated in 90 FR 10592 (Doc. 2025-03118): the rule 'requires that, to bear a claim subject to the rule, individual food products, mixed products, main dishes, and meals must meet FGEs and specific limits for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium based on a percentage of the Daily Value for these nutrients.' The food group equivalent requirement ensures the food contains meaningful amounts of nutrient-dense food groups, while the nutrient-to-limit requirement ensures the food does not contain excessive amounts of nutrients that should be limited in a healthy diet. Certain foods (e.g., single-ingredient foods from encouraged food groups with no added ingredients except water, and water/tea/coffee with less than 5 calories per RACC and per labeled serving) automatically qualify without meeting both criteria (89 FR 106064; 90 FR 10592).

answer_rows.required_change: Reformulate or verify that the product (1) contains the required food group equivalent (FGE) amount from Dietary Guidelines-encouraged food groups, and (2) does not exceed nutrient-to-limit (NTL) thresholds for added sugars, saturated fat, and sodium (as a percentage of Daily Value), unless the product qualifies for an automatic exemption.

response.answer: The 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim is governed by 21 CFR 101.65(d). This section defines the general nutritional claims paragraph that covers labeling claims using the term 'healthy' or related terms as implied nutrient content claims because they suggest that a food may help consumers maintain healthy dietary practices due to its nutrient content. The general principles for nutrient content claims (including the definition of implied nutrient content claims) are set forth in 21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii), which specifically identifies 'healthy' as an example of an implied nutrient content claim that 'suggests that a food, because of its nutrient content, may be useful in maintaining healthy dietary practices' (21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii), as amended by 89 FR 106064). The final rule updating the definition of 'healthy' was published on 2024-12-27 (89 FR 106064, Doc. 2024-29957), with an effective date of 2025-04-28 (as revised by Doc. 2025-03118) and a compliance date of 2028-02-25.

answer_rows.trigger: Final rule 2024-29957 (89 FR 106064) revising 21 CFR 101.65(d) definition of 'healthy'
answer_rows.required_change: Products must meet the updated food-group-equivalent-based criteria in revised 21 CFR 101.65(d)(3) (including nutrient limits per RACC in tables 2 and 3) to bear the 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim

response.answer: Your compliance date for the updated 'healthy' nutrient content claim rule is February 25, 2028. The final rule (89 FR 106064, Doc. 2024-29957) established a single compliance date of February 25, 2028, applicable to all regulated parties subject to the updated requirements under 21 CFR 101.65(d). FDA explicitly considered and rejected a request to provide small businesses with an extended compliance period (an additional 2 years beyond the general compliance date). In Response 135 of the preamble, FDA stated it did not have sufficient information to determine whether small businesses need additional time, and that extending the compliance date for small businesses could cause consumer confusion. Therefore, no size-based or revenue-based threshold exists in this rule — the February 25, 2028 compliance date applies uniformly regardless of your $8M annual sales figure. Note that while the effective date of the rule was delayed from February 25, 2025 to April 28, 2025 by Doc. 2025-03118 (90 FR 10592), that document explicitly states 'the compliance date remains unchanged at this time.'

answer_rows.trigger: Updated definition of 'healthy' implied nutrient content claim under 21 CFR 101.65(d)
answer_rows.required_change: Labeling bearing the 'healthy' claim must meet the new food-group-equivalent and nutrients-to-limit framework established by the final rule, or the claim must be removed

response.answer:
The revocation of FD&C Red No. 3 for use in food is governed by document 2025-00830 (90 FR 4628), published January 16, 2025. The key dates for food are as follows:

• Publication date: January 16, 2025 (90 FR 4628).

• Effective date: January 15, 2027. This is the date on which the listing at 21 CFR 74.303 (FD&C Red No. 3 for food use) is removed from the CFR. (2025-00830, amendatory instruction 2; timeline facts confirm this applies to 'All provisions except amendatory instruction 4.')

• Compliance date: None stated. The order sets no explicit compliance date for food. The operative deadline is derived from the effective date: once 21 CFR 74.303 is removed on January 15, 2027, food containing FD&C Red No. 3 would be adulterated because the color additive would no longer be listed for that use. Therefore the practical deadline for food manufacturers is January 15, 2027.

Note on the administrative stay: An administrative stay under 21 U.S.C. 371(e)(2) ran from February 18, 2025 through August 5, 2026 (per document 2026-15920). The timeline facts confirm the stay is no longer in force and that no dates were changed by the stay. The January 15, 2027 effective date remains as stated.

(The separate effective date of January 18, 2028 applies only to amendatory instruction 4, which removes 21 CFR 74.1303 — the listing for ingested drugs — and is not applicable to food.)

answer_rows.trigger: Removal of 21 CFR 74.303 (permanent listing of FD&C Red No. 3 for food use)
answer_rows.required_change: Reformulate to eliminate FD&C Red No. 3 from all food products; the color additive will no longer be listed for food use and any food containing it will be adulterated after the effective date.

response.answer: The updated 'healthy' nutrient content claim rule (89 FR 106064, Doc. 2024-29957) applies to the labeling of **human food** products. The rule establishes parameters for use of the term 'healthy' as an implied nutrient content claim 'on the label or in labeling of a food that suggests that a food, because of its nutrient content, may help consumers maintain healthy dietary practices' (2024-29957, § 101.65(d)(1) and (3)). The framework is built around food groups recommended in the Dietary Guidelines, 2020-2025 'for adults and children 2 years of age and older' (2025-03118#0003; 2024-29957#0005). The rule amends 21 CFR Part 101, which governs human food labeling. Dog treats are animal food, regulated under 21 CFR Part 501 (animal food labeling), not Part 101. Therefore, based on the sources provided, this rule does not apply to your dog treat product line. However, I cannot confirm from these sources alone whether a separate AAFCO or FDA Center for Veterinary Medicine (CVM) action might independently restrict use of 'healthy' on pet food labels; the sources here address only human food labeling under 21 CFR 101.65(d).

answer_rows.required_change: None under this rule — the updated 21 CFR 101.65(d) applies only to human food labeling, not animal food.

response.answer: Yes, you are affected. The final rule published at 89 FR 106064 (Doc. 2024-29957, published 2024-12-27) updates the definition of the implied nutrient content claim "healthy" under 21 CFR 101.65(d). Because your company makes a "healthy" claim, you must ensure your products meet the revised criteria by the stated compliance date. The rule's effective date was originally February 25, 2025, but was superseded to April 28, 2025 by document 2025-03118. The compliance date remains February 25, 2028, as stated in the final rule (89 FR 106064). By that date, any product bearing the "healthy" claim must conform to the updated food-group-based and nutrient-to-limit criteria in revised 21 CFR 101.65(d). The rule also revises 21 CFR 101.13(b)(2)(ii). Note that this is a voluntary claim—if a product cannot meet the new criteria, the claim must be removed rather than the product reformulated. FDA estimated that only a small number of products would need relabeling or reformulation (see Response 162 in the preamble, 89 FR 106064). No size threshold applies based on the documents in this corpus.

answer_rows.trigger: Updated definition of "healthy" nutrient content claim under 21 CFR 101.65(d)
answer_rows.required_change: Products must meet revised food-group and nutrient-to-limit criteria to bear the "healthy" claim, or the claim must be removed from labeling
